581.event_title: U-2 photographs and a lawful quarantine in the Cuban Missile Crisis
581.place: Cuba and Washington, D.C., United States
581.event: On 14 October 1962 an American U-2 reconnaissance aircraft photographed Soviet medium-range and intermediate-range ballistic missile sites under construction in Cuba, and analysts at the National Photographic Interpretation Center identified the missiles the next day. President John F. Kennedy and his advisers chose a naval quarantine rather than an immediate attack, using the word quarantine because a blockade would legally imply a state of war, and they sought the backing of the Organization of American States. Kennedy announced the quarantine on 22 October, and it was lifted on 20 November 1962 after the Soviet Union agreed to remove its missiles and, finally, its IL-28 bombers.
581.explanation: The crisis was handled with two kinds of sight working together: hard intelligence about what was actually happening, and careful attention to law and treaty about what the United States could rightfully do.
581.tie_back: The kural says a ruler has two eyes, spies who show what is happening and the respected books of law that show what ought to be done, and in October 1962 both eyes were open at once.
581._accuracy_note: A good modern match for the pairing of intelligence and legal principle; the kural's law books are ancient treatises on polity, here represented by international law and diplomacy.

582.event_title: Britain's Room 40 intercepts the Zimmermann Telegram
582.event: In January 1917 the German foreign secretary Arthur Zimmermann sent a coded telegram proposing that, if the United States entered the war, Mexico should ally with Germany. British naval codebreakers in Room 40 intercepted and decoded it as it passed over British-controlled cable routes. Britain passed the text to the American ambassador Walter Page on 22 February, its publication helped turn American opinion, and the United States declared war on Germany in April 1917.
582.explanation: Room 40 was reading not only enemy messages but the traffic that touched neutral countries, and so learned an enemy plan aimed at two neutrals before either of them knew of it.
582.tie_back: The kural makes it a ruler's duty to learn quickly what is happening with enemies, friends and neutrals alike, and the Zimmermann intercept shows that wide watchfulness turning the course of a war.
582._accuracy_note: A strong illustration of swift knowledge about enemies and neutrals together; the kural's ideal of knowing everything at all times is broader than any single intercept.

583.event_title: Stalin disregards warnings of the German invasion
583.event: In the months before June 1941, Soviet intelligence sources in Germany, Japan, Romania and Switzerland, including the spy Richard Sorge in Tokyo, reported that Germany was preparing to invade, and Churchill and Roosevelt also tried to warn Joseph Stalin. Stalin dismissed the reports as provocations or disinformation, kept supplying raw materials to Germany and ordered his forces not to fire on German aircraft crossing the border. On 22 June 1941 Germany launched Operation Barbarossa and inflicted massive early defeats on the unprepared Red Army.
583.explanation: Stalin did not lack intelligence; he failed to weigh it and draw the obvious conclusion, and his country paid an enormous price for that failure.
583.tie_back: The kural says a king who gathers news through spies but does not work out what it means has no path to victory, which is exactly what happened when Stalin's many warnings went unheeded.
583._accuracy_note: Nearly a dramatisation of the kural: intelligence was gathered but not understood; historians debate how clear every individual warning was, but not that Stalin ignored the overall picture.

584.event_title: The Venona project uncovers Soviet agents inside the US government
584.event: On 1 February 1943 the US Army's Signal Intelligence Service began a small, secret programme at Arlington Hall to study encrypted Soviet diplomatic and intelligence cables that had been collected since 1939. From 1946 the codebreaker Meredith Gardner and colleagues were able to read parts of messages showing that Soviet intelligence had sources inside the War Department, the atomic bomb project and other government agencies. Working with the FBI, the project, which ran until 1980, helped identify Klaus Fuchs, Julius Rosenberg and others, and the FBI says some 350 people connected with Soviet intelligence were identified.
584.explanation: The most dangerous leaks came not from open enemies but from trusted people inside the government's own offices and laboratories.
584.tie_back: The kural says a true intelligence service watches everyone without exception, the ruler's own officials as well as his enemies, and Venona found that some of the gravest threats sat among America's own officials.
584._accuracy_note: A strong fit for watching one's own officials as closely as enemies; the kural also names the king's relatives, which Venona does not touch.

585.event_title: Virginia Hall, the Limping Lady, works undetected in occupied France
585.event: Virginia Hall, an American who had lost her lower left leg in a hunting accident and walked with an artificial limb, became the British Special Operations Executive's first female resident agent in France in 1941. The Gestapo circulated wanted posters for her, and when her network was compromised she escaped over the Pyrenees on foot. In 1944 she returned for the American Office of Strategic Services, disguised as an elderly French farmwoman, and organised resistance and sabotage while reporting German troop movements; the Gestapo never caught her.
585.explanation: Hall's ordinary, unremarkable appearance and her steady nerve let one of the most wanted Allied agents move freely through occupied territory.
585.tie_back: The kural describes the true spy as having an appearance that draws no suspicion, not flinching under watchful eyes and never letting a secret slip, all of which Hall did in occupied France.
585._accuracy_note: Matches all three qualities in the kural closely; she was briefly interned in Spain after her escape, though never captured by the Germans.

586.event_title: Nain Singh surveys Tibet disguised as a Buddhist pilgrim
586.event: Nain Singh, one of the Indian surveyors known as pundits who were trained by the Survey of India, set out in 1865 to map Tibet, which was then closed to outsiders. Travelling disguised as a Buddhist pilgrim and trader, he counted his paces on a rosary of 100 beads instead of the usual 108, hid notes and a compass in a prayer wheel and concealed instruments in his baggage, reaching Lhasa in 1866. He fixed the position and altitude of Lhasa and mapped a long stretch of the trade route, and the Royal Geographical Society later awarded him its Patron's Medal.
586.explanation: By taking the outward form of a pilgrim, Nain Singh entered a country that no ordinary surveyor could enter and brought back accurate information without ever being exposed.
586.tie_back: The kural describes the spy who takes on the guise of a renunciant, enters places others cannot reach, examines them thoroughly and never gives himself away, which is almost exactly Nain Singh's journey.
586._accuracy_note: Almost a dramatisation: a disguise as a religious traveller, entry into a closed land, careful observation and secrecy; his work was geographical survey for the British, which was itself a form of intelligence gathering.

587.event_title: Marian Rejewski breaks the German Enigma machine
587.event: At the end of 1932 Marian Rejewski, a young mathematician in the Polish Cipher Bureau, used mathematical methods to reconstruct the wiring of the German military Enigma machine, and with Jerzy Rozycki and Henryk Zygalski he went on to read German Enigma messages through the 1930s. In 1938 the team built a device called the bomba to help find daily settings. In July 1939, at Pyry near Warsaw, Polish intelligence handed over its methods and reconstructed Enigma machines to British and French representatives.
587.explanation: Rejewski drew out secrets that Germany believed to be beyond reach, and did so with mathematical rigour that left no doubt about the results.
587.tie_back: The kural describes the spy who can draw out what is hidden and has no doubt about what he has found, and Rejewski's reconstruction of Enigma met both standards.
587._accuracy_note: A strong fit for uncovering hidden secrets with certainty; Rejewski was a codebreaker rather than a field spy, so the kural's human-agent setting is translated into signals intelligence.

588.event_title: American codebreakers confirm that AF means Midway
588.place: Pearl Harbor, Hawaii, and Midway Atoll
588.event: In spring 1942 US Navy codebreakers at Station Hypo in Pearl Harbor, led by Joseph Rochefort, read Japanese messages referring to an objective called AF and suspected it was Midway, but analysts in Washington doubted this. To test the reading, the Navy had Midway report by secure cable and then broadcast an uncoded message that its fresh-water plant had broken down. When a Japanese intelligence report soon stated that AF was short of water, the identification was confirmed, and the US Navy prepared the ambush that won the Battle of Midway in June 1942.
588.explanation: Rather than act on a single reading of intercepted traffic, the Navy found an independent way to check it before staking the Pacific Fleet on it.
588.tie_back: The kural says that even information a spy has brought in should be accepted only after it has been checked by another, and the water-shortage test was exactly such a second check.
588._accuracy_note: A very close fit for verifying intelligence by an independent check; sources differ on whether the test was mainly meant to convince Washington or Admiral Nimitz.

589.event_title: Independent reports and air photographs confirm the German rocket site at Peenemunde
589.place: Peenemunde, Germany, and RAF Medmenham, England
589.event: From 1939 British intelligence received scattered reports, including the anonymous Oslo Report, that Germany was developing long-range rockets and other secret weapons, but these were at first doubted. Reports from other sources pointed to Peenemunde on the Baltic coast, and photo-reconnaissance flights between 1942 and 1943 were examined by interpreters at RAF Medmenham, where Constance Babington Smith's section searched for secret weapons. When separate lines of intelligence and the aerial photographs agreed, Bomber Command attacked Peenemunde on the night of 17-18 August 1943 in Operation Hydra.
589.explanation: No single report was trusted on its own; action came only when separate, unconnected sources told the same story.
589.tie_back: The kural says to use agents who do not know of one another and to trust a matter when their separate reports agree, which is how Britain confirmed the threat from Peenemunde before striking it.
589._accuracy_note: Illustrates corroboration by independent sources; the sources were a mix of human reports and photo-reconnaissance rather than the kural's three mutually unaware spies.

590.event_title: Double agent Garbo receives his MBE in secret
590.event: Juan Pujol Garcia, codenamed Garbo, was a Spanish double agent run by MI5 who fed the Germans false reports from an imaginary network of agents, helping convince them that the main Allied invasion would come at the Pas de Calais rather than Normandy. In July 1944 the Germans awarded him the Iron Cross, still believing he worked for them. In December 1944 the British awarded him the MBE, presented by MI5's Director General, but in secret to avoid exposing him, and his identity as Garbo was not publicly uncovered until 1984.
590.explanation: Britain honoured one of its most valuable agents while making sure that no one outside a tiny circle knew it, protecting both the man and the deception.
590.tie_back: The kural warns a ruler not to honour a spy where others can see, lest he himself reveal the secret, and Garbo's private MBE followed that counsel to the letter.
590._accuracy_note: Almost a dramatisation of the kural: the agent was rewarded, but deliberately in secret so as not to expose him.
